title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a well-documented one: a generative AI tool asserting nonexistent legal authorities as fact. An attorney submitted court filings containing seven case citations that did not exist, along with fabricated quotes and false legal holdings. The error entered the record across eight separate filings before it was caught and admitted. The failure happened at the drafting stage, before any human verification of the cited sources took place.

The attorney believed the AI tool she used, called Irys, was connected to her law firm's existing legal research subscription, a connection that was not established. That misunderstanding removed the friction that might otherwise have prompted independent verification. A check as simple as confirming each cited case in a primary legal database would have caught the fabrications before filing.

What is not established is whether the underlying AI tool was defective in an unusual way, whether any court sanction has yet been issued in this matter, or whether State Farm directed or was aware of the AI use. The admissions by the attorneys are not a judicial finding on liability for the broader insurance dispute, which remained scheduled for trial.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have apologized for using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in their court filings. The case involves homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, a storm caused water damage, and Meni-Siliga claims State Farm delayed approving repairs, ultimately leading her family to lose their home to foreclosure and declare bankruptcy. State Farm attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, and she incorrectly thought an AI tool called Irys was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription.

The use of AI in law has become widespread, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments using generative AI. A worldwide database has documented 1,922 cases of AI-generated legal hallucinations, with most occurring in the United States. A California attorney was previously fined a record ten thousand dollars for using ChatGPT in a brief containing 21 made-up quotes. Meni-Siliga's case is scheduled to go to trial in October.
